title: Space Robots Need a Tune-Up: Why AI Isn't Ready to Fly a Spaceship
summary:
Imagine a spaceship where robots do everything. They scrub floors, fix engines, and drive you around in floating chairs. That's the starship Axiom in the movie WALL-E. Its AI, named AUTO, runs the whole ship for 700 years. Pretty cool, right? Well, real space robots are not there yet.

Today's AI is more like a helpful sidekick than a captain. NASA and the European Space Agency use it to drive Mars rovers, stop satellites from crashing, and train astronauts. But it still messes up. Ever asked ChatGPT something and gotten a made-up answer? That's called a hallucination. In space, mistakes are a big deal. "You have virtually no room for error," says Daniele Gammelli, a scientist at Stanford University.

The Mars rover Perseverance uses AI to scan rocks and decide which ones to collect. The rover Curiosity uses AI to zap rocks with lasers. Both work without humans telling them every move. That's handy, because people get overwhelmed by huge amounts of data.

So what's next? Scientists want robots that can make their own small goals and handle surprises, like WALL-E did when he used a fire extinguisher to escape. But for now, humans stay in charge. Would you trust a robot with your life in space? Probably not yet!
why_it_matters: AI is showing up in phones, cars, and classrooms, so learning when to trust a robot's answer — and when a human should double-check it — is a skill you will use your whole life.

background_read: WALL-E is an animated movie about a lonely trash-collecting robot left behind on a polluted Earth, while humans live far away on a huge spaceship run by machines.
The European Space Agency (a group of European countries that work together on space missions) and NASA both use computer programs to help control spacecraft far from Earth.
Stanford University (a famous university in California, USA) is one of many places where scientists study how to make AI safer and more reliable.
Article_Structure: WHO: NASA, the European Space Agency, and scientists like Daniele Gammelli at Stanford University — plus the movie AI AUTO from WALL-E.
WHAT: Real AI already helps space robots work, but it still makes mistakes like hallucinations, so humans stay in charge.
WHERE: On Earth in labs and control rooms, and in space — on Mars with rovers like Perseverance and Curiosity, and in orbit around Earth with satellites.
WHY: In space there is almost no room for error, so scientists need robots that can handle surprises before they can be trusted to run a mission alone.

perspectives.description: AI lets rovers and satellites do useful work without humans giving every single command, which saves time and helps handle huge amounts of data.
If AI can make up a wrong answer here on Earth, a wrong decision in space could ruin an expensive mission, so letting robots decide things alone still feels risky.
Researchers want robots that can set small goals and deal with surprises, like WALL-E escaping with a fire extinguisher — but until then, humans will keep their hands on the controls.
